summary:
Glacier Pulse is an interactive glacier-monitoring and exploration platform designed to make satellite data more accessible and understandable. It uses observations from NASA–ISRO's NISAR mission, particularly Geocoded Offset (GOFF) products, alongside the Randolph Glacier Inventory to explore Himalayan glaciers.

We developed a map-based Glacier Explorer, NISAR Radar Lab, measurement visualizations, glacier comparison tools and an AI-powered interpreter that explains complex scientific data in simpler language. The platform extracts and visualizes radar displacement measurements, such as along-track and slant-range offsets, together with quality indicators like correlation and signal-to-noise information.

Glacier Pulse addresses the challenge of understanding glacier changes by transforming complex satellite measurements into accessible visual insights. It is important because glaciers influence freshwater availability, mountain ecosystems and communities downstream. By making Earth observation data easier to explore and interpret, Glacier Pulse aims to support scientific awareness and informed discussion about changing glaciers.
details:
Project Details – Glacier Pulse

Every Glacier Has a Story

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Glacier Pulse is an interactive glacier-monitoring and exploration platform focused on making satellite-based glacier observations easier to understand. It uses data from NASA–ISRO's NISAR mission, particularly Geocoded Offset (GOFF) products, together with the Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI 7.0), to explore Himalayan glaciers.

The platform searches and accesses available satellite products through the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF). It processes GOFF data to extract along-track and slant-range offsets, correlation measurements, signal-to-noise information and other quality indicators. These measurements are displayed through colour-coded visualizations, statistical summaries and interactive maps.

Users can explore glacier locations and boundaries, inspect radar measurements, understand data quality and learn about the scientific meaning of the observations through accessible explanations. An AI-powered Glacier Interpreter is designed to translate complex scientific information into simpler language.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Makes satellite data accessible: Converts complex radar measurements into understandable visual information.
  • Supports glacier awareness: Helps users explore changes and observations in Himalayan glacier regions.
  • Encourages scientific learning: Introduces users to satellite remote sensing, radar measurements and glacier monitoring.
  • Improves data interpretation: Displays measurement-quality indicators so users can understand the reliability and limitations of observations.
  • Connects science with society: Helps communicate why glaciers matter to freshwater resources, ecosystems and downstream communities.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make glacier observation more accessible to students, researchers, educators and the general public. Himalayan glaciers are important components of regional water systems and mountain ecosystems. Understanding their changing conditions is essential for raising awareness about environmental change and its potential consequences.

Glacier Pulse aims to bridge the gap between advanced Earth observation technology and public understanding. It can serve as an educational and exploratory platform and provide a foundation for more advanced glacier analysis as additional satellite observations and scientific processing become available.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware and software did you use?

Programming languages and frontend:

  • JavaScript
  • React
  • Vite
  • HTML and CSS

Backend and data processing:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • NumPy and scientific data-processing libraries
  • HDF5 data handling for NISAR products

Mapping and visualization:

  • Leaflet for interactive maps
  • Geospatial visualization of glacier boundaries and radar measurements
  • Colour-coded offset maps and statistical summaries

Data sources and infrastructure:

  • NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite mission
  • Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) for satellite data discovery and access
  • Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI 7.0) for glacier reference outlines
  • Cloudflare Pages for frontend deployment
  • Render for backend hosting
  • Cloudflare R2 for storing glacier inventory data

The project primarily uses satellite observations and cloud-based computing infrastructure rather than requiring dedicated satellite hardware.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of Glacier Pulse is the way it transforms complex scientific radar measurements into an interactive and understandable experience.

Instead of presenting users with raw satellite files and technical metadata, it combines:

  • A map-first glacier exploration experience.
  • A radar laboratory for visualizing real GOFF measurements.
  • Statistical summaries that explain the distribution of displacement measurements.
  • Measurement-quality indicators that help users assess radar pattern matching and signal clarity.
  • An AI-powered interpreter that explains technical concepts in everyday language.
  • A glacier-focused interface connecting scientific observations with environmental awareness.

The platform brings satellite data discovery, scientific visualization and public education together in one experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Scientific accuracy and responsible interpretation were central considerations throughout development.

  • Data reliability: Correlation, signal-to-noise information and measurement uncertainty must be considered when interpreting radar offsets.
  • Scientific limitations: Radar-coordinate offsets must not be presented as direct glacier velocity or ice loss without the required geometric transformations and further analysis.
  • Geographic accuracy: Satellite observation footprints must be checked before associating a data product with a specific glacier.
  • Data availability: Satellite products may differ in coverage, acquisition dates and processing maturity.
  • Accessibility: The interface should be understandable to people without a background in remote sensing.
  • Performance: Large satellite datasets require efficient processing, visualization and cloud storage.
  • Transparency: Historical glacier outlines and recent satellite observations must be distinguished clearly.
  • Scalability: The architecture should support additional glaciers, satellite observations and future scientific analysis.

Conclusion

Glacier Pulse aims to turn advanced satellite Earth observation into accessible knowledge. By combining NISAR radar measurements, glacier reference data, interactive visualization and AI-assisted explanations, we want to help more people explore the stories hidden in glacier observations. Our vision is to make glacier science easier to understand while maintaining the scientific integrity that meaningful environmental monitoring requires.
